quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Incident Review: Online Ordering Outage, 12 March] Summary. On 12 March, customers were unable to place orders for 3 hours and 40 minutes, beginning at 6:05 p.m., the busiest period of the week. Roughly 4,100 orders were lost or delayed. Timeline. At 5:50 p.m., an engineer deployed a routine update to the discount-code system. At 6:05 p.m., the order page began returning errors; the monitoring system generated an alert, but it was sent to a mailbox that is checked only during office hours. The first sign that anything was wrong came at 6:32 p.m., when a customer-service agent noticed a surge of complaint calls and escalated it by telephone. Engineers identified the update as the likely cause at 7:10 p.m. but initially hesitated to reverse it, because a reversal would also remove a security fix that had been included in the same release. After a discussion between the engineering and security teams, the update was reversed at 9:25 p.m., and the security fix was reapplied separately by 9:45 p.m. Contributing factors. The update was released at a time of peak demand, which the deployment guidelines discourage but do not prohibit. The alert system worked as designed, but the destination was not appropriate for an urgent warning. Two unrelated changes had been bundled into one release, which complicated the decision to reverse it. Actions. Alerts will be routed to the on-call engineer's phone. Releases will be prohibited between 5:00 and 9:00 p.m. on weekdays. Security fixes will be released separately from other changes.
quests.question: Which factor most directly delayed the first response to the outage?
options: The alert was sent to a mailbox checked only in office hours.
Engineers could not identify the update.
The monitoring system failed to detect the errors.
The customer-service team did not escalate the problem.
quests.correctAnswer: The alert was sent to a mailbox checked only in office hours.
quests.hint: Compare when the errors began with when anyone noticed.
quests.explanation: The system raised an alert at 6:05, but it went to a mailbox no one watches in the evening, so the first human notice came at 6:32 from a phone call.
quests.evidenceLine: checked only during office hours

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Two Views on Short-Term Rentals] Councillor Dara Voss (supporting a ban on whole-home rentals under 30 days): "In our old town, one in six homes is now a holiday rental. Families who grew up here cannot find homes, because landlords make more renting by the night than by the year. Schools in the old town have lost a third of their pupils in a decade, and last year the council received more than 300 complaints about noise and rubbish from residents living beside holiday lets. Hosts say they depend on this income, and I believe them, but the community cannot be run as an extension of the tourism industry. A ban would return around 900 homes to the long-term market." Mr. Ibrahim Sayed (opposing the ban): "The ban would be a blunt tool. Most hosts are not investors; they are residents renting a spare room or their own home while they travel. A ban on whole-home rentals would catch them too. Meanwhile, the real driver of high rents is the shortage of new housing, which this council has failed to address for twenty years. Banning rentals would cost the local economy an estimated $14 million a year in visitor spending, and there is no guarantee that landlords would rent to locals instead of leaving homes empty or selling to second-home buyers."
quests.question: How do the speakers differ on the cause of high rents?
options: Both speakers blame the shortage of new housing in the area.
Voss blames holiday rentals; Sayed blames a shortage of new housing.
Voss blames the council's planners, while Sayed blames tourists.
Both speakers blame second-home buyers for the high rents.
quests.correctAnswer: Voss blames holiday rentals; Sayed blames a shortage of new housing.
quests.hint: Look for the explanation each speaker gives of why locals cannot find homes.
quests.explanation: Voss says landlords earn more from nightly rentals; Sayed says the real driver is the lack of new housing.
quests.evidenceLine: the real driver of high rents is the shortage of new housing

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Sunday Dinner] Naomi had rehearsed three topics of conversation in the car, and so far she had used none of them. Luka's mother passed the potatoes with the air of someone handing over evidence. "Luka tells me you changed jobs again," she said. "He tells me you're an adviser now. For whom?" "A small firm," said Naomi. "We help schools plan their budgets." "Schools," repeated Mrs. Varga. "Well. That's steady." Across the table, Luka's father cleared his throat and asked whether anyone had seen the match on Saturday. Nobody had. He seemed relieved to have been refused. The potatoes, Naomi noticed, had gone cold. "Luka says you grew up near the coast," Mrs. Varga continued. "Is your family there still?" "My mother is," said Naomi. "She'd like to meet you both, sometime." It was the first sentence she had planned, and she had not expected it to land the way it did. Mrs. Varga's fork paused. Then she smiled, a real one, small and a little surprised. "I would like that," she said, "very much." Luka, who had been studying his plate as if it contained instructions, looked up for the first time in ten minutes. Neither woman mentioned jobs again for the rest of the meal; the conversation moved, tentatively, to coastlines, ferries and the best way to cook fish.
quests.question: What is implied by Mrs. Varga's remark "Well. That's steady"?
options: Complete admiration for Naomi's work with the schools and budgets
Strong disapproval of the idea of working with schools
Cautious approval, with doubt about Naomi's earlier job changes
Amusement at the idea of working for such a small firm
quests.correctAnswer: Cautious approval, with doubt about Naomi's earlier job changes
quests.hint: Read the remark together with her earlier comment about changing jobs "again".
quests.explanation: She approves of a stable job, but "steady" in this context suggests she is contrasting it with Naomi's earlier job changes.
quests.evidenceLine: Luka tells me you changed jobs again

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Living Below the Sea] About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, and roughly a third is vulnerable to flooding from the sea or from rivers. The country's survival depends on an interlocking system rather than any single defense. Dikes, the earthen or concrete embankments that run along the coast and rivers, are the most visible element. But dikes alone cannot protect low land from rainwater and groundwater, which collect inside them. For centuries, windmills pumped this water out; today, electric pumping stations do the same, lifting it into canals and rivers that carry it to the sea. After a catastrophic North Sea flood in 1953 killed more than 1,800 people, the government built a series of enormous barriers, the Delta Works, designed to withstand storms expected only once in ten thousand years. One barrier, the Maeslantkering, closes only when a major storm surge is forecast. The Dutch approach has begun to change. Engineers now speak of "room for the river" rather than simply raising dikes: lowering floodplains, relocating some farms, and creating spillways that allow rivers to flood harmlessly in designated areas. The reasoning is that higher walls push the water elsewhere, and that rising seas and heavier rainfall will eventually overwhelm any barrier built too confidently. Living with water, rather than defeating it, has become official policy.
quests.question: Why are dikes alone not enough to protect low land?
options: Rainwater and groundwater collect inside them and must be pumped out.
Dikes are too expensive for the government to maintain every year.
Dikes cannot be seen clearly from the sea during storms.
Dikes are always too short to hold back the sea in storms.
quests.correctAnswer: Rainwater and groundwater collect inside them and must be pumped out.
quests.hint: Look at the sentence that begins with "But".
quests.explanation: Dikes keep out sea and river water, but water that falls or seeps inside them has to be pumped away.
quests.evidenceLine: dikes alone cannot protect low land from rainwater and groundwater

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Travel Insurance Claim Conditions: Cancellation Cover] Cancellation cover reimburses non-refundable trip costs if you must cancel for a covered reason. Covered reasons are: serious illness or injury of the insured person or a close relative, death of a close relative, jury service, redundancy of the insured person where they have been employed continuously for at least two years, and damage to the insured person's home making it uninhabitable. Voluntary changes of plan, fear of travelling, and cancellation because of a pre-existing medical condition are not covered unless the condition was declared and accepted by the insurer when the policy was purchased. You must notify the insurer within 48 hours of the event that forces you to cancel, and you must tell the travel provider immediately, since claims will be reduced if costs increase through delay. A medical certificate is required for any illness-related claim. Claims for trips booked through a travel agent must also include the agent's written confirmation of the booking date. The maximum payment is $4,000 per person, and the first $150 of every claim is deducted as an excess. Close relative means a spouse, parent, child, brother or sister, grandparent or grandchild. If the policy was purchased more than 14 days after the trip was booked, cover for cancellation due to illness begins only after a seven-day waiting period.
quests.question: A traveler's non-refundable costs are $3,000. She cancels because her mother falls seriously ill, and all conditions are met. What will she receive?
quests.hint: Remember that every claim has an excess.
quests.explanation: The claim is covered and below the maximum, but the first $150 is deducted, so she receives $2,850.
quests.evidenceLine: the first $150 of every claim is deducted as an excess

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Restaurant Review: The Second Visit] When I first reviewed Brasa in 2021, I called it the most exciting opening of the year. The chef, Ana Duarte, cooked over open fire with a confidence that made even the vegetables memorable, and I left wanting to return the next night. So it is with some reluctance that I report a very different experience this spring. Duarte left in January, and her successor, the capable but cautious Tomas Weil, has kept the menu while quietly sanding down its edges. The famous charred cabbage now arrives pale and polite. A lamb dish, once seasoned so boldly that it started conversations, tasted of very little beyond itself. Nothing was wrong, exactly, and that is the problem: the kitchen now cooks as though it were afraid of complaints. Service remains excellent, and the room is as warm as ever. The wine list, at least, remains as interesting and fairly priced as before. I do not doubt that Weil is talented, and some of his own additions, a tart of leeks and sheep's cheese in particular, hinted at what he could do if allowed to stop imitating. But a restaurant that was once an argument has become a reassurance. For the prices charged, I expect more than reassurance. I will return in the autumn, in the hope that Weil has found his own voice.
quests.question: What is the reviewer's main criticism of the restaurant now?
options: The service has become slow, poor and sometimes rude.
The dining room has lost its warmth and atmosphere.
The menu has been completely replaced by the new chef.
The cooking has become timid and lost its distinct character.
quests.correctAnswer: The cooking has become timid and lost its distinct character.
quests.hint: The reviewer says that "nothing was wrong, exactly"; find what the problem is instead.
quests.explanation: The dishes are the same on paper but have been softened, and the kitchen seems afraid of complaints.
quests.evidenceLine: the kitchen now cooks as though it were afraid of complaints

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Pricing Decision at Page & Co.] Page & Co., an independent bookstore, sells new paperbacks at the publisher's recommended price. Faced with competition from an online retailer, the owner, Helen Brandt, considered a 15 percent discount on all paperbacks. Her accountant estimated that the store's average margin on paperbacks was 40 percent before the discount. The discount would therefore reduce the margin on each book to 25 percent of the original price, a drop of more than a third in profit per book. To break even on total profit, she calculated, sales would need to rise by 60 percent. A survey of 200 customers suggested that the discount might raise purchases by about a quarter, far short of what was needed. Her accountant also reminded her that rent and wages would not fall. However, the survey also revealed that customers valued things the online retailer could not offer: staff recommendations, a children's reading corner, and the ability to hold a book before buying. Instead of discounting, Brandt decided to invest in these features, adding two evening events a month and a small subscription service in which staff choose a book for members. The online retailer's prices remained lower throughout. After a year, paperback sales were unchanged but subscription income had added the equivalent of 9 percent to annual profit, and she had not touched her prices.
quests.question: Why would the discount require a 60 percent rise in sales to break even?
options: Customers would stop buying other items once the discount ended.
Profit per book would fall from 40 to 25 percent of the price.
The cost of buying the books from publishers would increase.
The online retailer would match the discount within a week.
quests.correctAnswer: Profit per book would fall from 40 to 25 percent of the price.
quests.hint: Compare the profit per book before and after the discount.
quests.explanation: Profit per book would drop from 40 to 25 percent of the original price, so about 60 percent more books would be needed to earn the same total.
quests.evidenceLine: reduce the margin on each book to 25 percent of the original price

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [The Penny Post] Before 1840, sending a letter in Britain was expensive and strange. The recipient, not the sender, paid, and the cost depended on distance and the number of sheets. A letter from London to Edinburgh could cost a laborer a day's wages. Unsurprisingly, people found ways around the system: families agreed on codes written on the outside of the envelope, which the recipient could read and refuse to accept, thereby receiving the news for free. Rowland Hill, a schoolteacher turned reformer, argued in 1837 that the high prices were self-defeating. He observed that the actual cost of carrying a letter was a tiny fraction of the charge, and that the expensive bureaucracy of calculating and collecting fees consumed most of the difference. His proposal was radical: a uniform rate of one penny for any letter under a certain weight, paid in advance by the sender with an adhesive stamp. The Post Office resisted, and some officials predicted financial disaster. When the scheme began in 1840, however, the volume of letters rose from about 76 million a year to more than 160 million within two years. Revenue initially fell but recovered within a decade as the volume grew. Hill's reform shows that a price which seems generous can sometimes produce more, not less, for the one who sets it.
quests.question: Why did families write codes on the outside of envelopes?
options: To protect the privacy of the letter's contents
To save paper by writing the news on the envelope
To get the news without paying, by refusing the letter
To show off their writing skills to the postman
quests.correctAnswer: To get the news without paying, by refusing the letter
quests.hint: Remember who paid for letters before 1840.
quests.explanation: The recipient paid, so a coded message on the envelope let them learn the news and then refuse the letter.
quests.evidenceLine: refuse to accept, thereby receiving the news for free

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [A Year of Teaching Adults to Read] I began volunteering at the literacy program expecting to be useful in a straightforward way. I would be the person who knew the alphabet, and my students would be the people who did not. This turned out to be wrong in almost every particular. My first student, Mr. Adeyemi, was a sixty-year-old builder who had managed a crew of twelve for decades without reading a single contract, relying instead on a memory so reliable that it frightened his accountant. He did not need me to explain the world. He needed me to explain the page. Over the year, I learned how elaborate the workarounds of non-readers can be: bringing a child to appointments, claiming to have forgotten glasses, nodding at forms and taking them home. Each was a small act of intelligence, and each had a cost in shame that the person carried alone. Mr. Adeyemi's first complete sentence, which he read aloud in March, was "The foreman has left the site." He read it with such concentration that I realized I had never seen anyone so frightened of a six-word sentence, or so determined to finish it. We both pretended not to notice that his eyes were wet. In June he read his first contract, slowly, and found an error that his accountant had missed. He did not say anything. He simply circled it with a pencil and slid it across the table, grinning.
quests.question: How does the writer's view of the students change?
options: From admiration for the students to growing boredom with the lessons
From pity for the students to resentment of their stubborn pride
From confusion about the program to anger at its organizers and rules
From assuming they lacked ability to seeing their resourcefulness and shame
quests.correctAnswer: From assuming they lacked ability to seeing their resourcefulness and shame
quests.hint: Compare the writer's opening expectation with the conclusions drawn in the middle of the passage.
quests.explanation: The writer began expecting to supply what students lacked but came to see their workarounds as intelligence, carried with shame.
quests.evidenceLine: Each was a small act of intelligence

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Letters about a Faulty Laptop] Letter from customer: "I bought a laptop from your store on 3 February. On 19 July the screen began flickering, and by August it would not turn on. The laptop is covered by a two-year manufacturer's warranty, but when I called your service department I was told that it could not be repaired under warranty because it had been 'subjected to liquid damage.' I have never spilled anything on it. I would like a replacement or a refund." Reply from the company: "Thank you for your letter. Our technician has examined your laptop and found corrosion on the main board consistent with liquid exposure. Such damage is excluded from the manufacturer's warranty. We appreciate that you do not recall any spillage, and we are not suggesting you have been dishonest; high humidity or a small amount of condensation can sometimes produce similar corrosion. However, the exclusion applies regardless of how the exposure occurred. As a gesture of goodwill, we can offer to repair the laptop at cost, which we estimate at $210, a saving of about 40 percent on our usual charge. Alternatively, you may wish to ask your home insurer whether the damage would be covered. We value your custom and hope to resolve this to your satisfaction. Please let us know your preference within 14 days."
quests.question: What is the central disagreement between the customer and the company?
options: Whether the laptop was bought on 3 February
Whether the fault is covered by the warranty
How long the warranty lasts
Whether a technician examined the laptop
quests.correctAnswer: Whether the fault is covered by the warranty
quests.hint: Look at what the customer says she was told and what the company replies.
quests.explanation: The customer says it should be repaired under warranty, but the company says liquid damage is excluded from it.
quests.evidenceLine: Such damage is excluded from the manufacturer's warranty
